Choosing a resolution

Justin Chase

19 October 2026

Source: vignettes/resolution.Rmd
resolution.Rmd

This article needs two optional packages: gstat, which fits the variogram behind the autocorrelation range, and ggplot2 for the figures. When either is missing the code is shown but not run, and a note at the top says so.

The question

Before point observations can be aggregated into regions, something has to decide how many regions. Twenty cells over a county smooth away most of the variation you came to measure. Two thousand give you cells holding one observation each, where the standard errors are undefined and every cell mean is one number pretending to be an average.

Administrative boundaries settle this by fiat: you get the census tracts that exist. Drawing the regions yourself removes the fiat and leaves the decision with you, and the number propagates into the variance of the cell means, the design effect, and the size of the blocks a spatial cross-validation holds out.

Three functions answer the question, in increasing order of how much they tell you. determine_optimal_levels() reads an elbow off the coordinates alone and runs on the hard dependencies; it is the quick answer and the one build_tessellation() accepts directly. resolution_profile() scores every cell count on a ladder in five columns at once, four count criteria and one diagnostic, and needs gstat for two of them. select_resolution() reads one criterion off that profile, and summary() on the profile reads the count criteria side by side. If the cells will feed a model, the profile is the one to use. If you need a count now and the data are all you have, the elbow is defensible when the points cluster, and this article says where it falls short. On points spread evenly there is no elbow to read, and both functions say so: the profile leaves its elbow column empty, and determine_optimal_levels() warns that the count it still returns was chosen by the ends of its ladder, not by the data.

Called with the response and nothing else, resolution_profile() takes its defaults: one level at 4.5 observations per cell, scored for the pooled value that summarize_by_cell() reports by default, in density-weighted cells, with no variogram fitted. select_resolution() then reads the count off that size (“Setting a size” below). A ladder argument such as n_levels gives the ladder this article reads first. Each earlier default is one argument away: estimate = NULL, obs_per_cell = NULL in the profile for the ladder without the pooled value’s columns, sac = NULL for a variogram on a ladder of sizes, partition = "kmeans" for k-means cells from 25 starts, criterion = "cp" in select_resolution(), and estimate = "mean" in summarize_by_cell().

The argument that says “how many” is spelled differently by the function it belongs to: max_levels bounds the elbow’s ladder, n_levels sets the profile’s and obs_per_cell sets it in observations per cell, approx_n_cells and target_cells are what the grid builders take, and n is what get_voronoi_seeds() takes. Each of the last three accepts the object the first two return.

A fixture with known structure

A simulated exponential field, so the structure is known before anything is fitted. The covariance parameter a = 100 gives an effective range of 300 units across a 1000-unit square, and sd = 1 adds a nugget large enough to matter later.

library(sf)
library(spatialkit)

set.seed(42)
n  <- 500
xy <- data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000))
D  <- as.matrix(dist(xy))
xy$z <- as.numeric(t(chol(exp(-D / 100) + diag(1e-8, n))) %*% rnorm(n)) +
        rnorm(n, sd = 1)
pts  <- st_as_sf(xy, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)

The short answer

determine_optimal_levels() returns a few candidate cell counts, best first.

lv <- determine_optimal_levels(pts, max_levels = 40)
lv
## [1] 7 6 8

This fixture’s points are uniform, so their within-cluster sum of squares falls like c / k all the way down and bends nowhere of its own. The call warns that it found no elbow and that max_levels chose lv: a larger max_levels would give a larger answer. Read an elbow only off points that cluster; here the profile below is the better guide.

lv[1] is what get_voronoi_seeds() takes as n, and what build_tessellation() takes as approx_n_cells for its "hex" and "square" methods. Voronoi has no cell count to set: it grows one cell per point you hand it, which is why the count is set when you place the seeds rather than when you tessellate them. The last section shows the two calls in order.

Two things to know about this function before you rely on it. Its criterion = "morans_i" and criterion = "combined" settings rank the counts around the elbow by Moran’s z of the cell means, which is a diagnostic and not a count rule; the call returns the ranking with a warning of class spatialkit_diagnostic_ranking that says so. They need a response_var; without one the call warns and falls back to "geometric". And its ladder runs from 1 to max_levels with no lower bound from the spatial correlation of the data, so it can prefer cells wider than the field’s own correlation range. The profile below reports that bound, and select_resolution() reads reliability from it up, which is why the two can disagree.

The profile

resolution_profile() fits every level on a ladder and reports what each one costs, so you can see the shape of the trade-off before picking a point on it. n_levels asks for that ladder. Levels are spaced logarithmically, because cell diameter falls as L−1/2L^{-1/2}. At its defaults the profile also scores the leave-one-out error of the pooled value, loo, at every level, and draws the cells by density-weighted k-means.

prof <- resolution_profile(pts, response_var = "z", n_levels = 16)
prof

One row per level. cell_n_median and cell_diam_median are usually the first two columns worth reading: how many points a typical cell holds, and how big it is in CRS units. cell_diam_median is twice the median root-mean-square distance of a cell’s points from its centre, about 0.8 of the side of a square cell of the same area, so compare it against something you already know about your own data, such as the spacing of a sampling grid or the size of a field, with that factor in mind.

Four criteria and a diagnostic

criterion measures needs direction
elbow how far the log of the within-cluster sum of squares sags below a power law (the straight log-log line from one cell to the last level); NA at every level when the points have no cluster structure coordinates only larger
cp Mallows’ CpC_p of the piecewise-constant approximation of the response by cell means a response, and a variogram for the nugget smaller
moran_z Moran’s z of the cell means (of their regression residuals when predictors are given): whether neighbouring cells resemble each other a response a diagnostic, not a count rule
reliability the share of the spread in the cell means that is signal, not sampling noise a variogram larger
loo the leave-one-out error of the cell value the profile scores, the pooled value by default (“Setting a size”) a response smaller

elbow sees the coordinates and knows nothing about what you measured. cp and reliability split the practical question in half: how well the cells represent the field, and whether the cell values can be told apart from noise. What cp estimates is the error of re-measuring the sampled sites, each predicted by the mean of its cell, with the variogram’s nugget as the noise of one measurement. For a new location the penalty would also need the spread of the field inside a cell, which the nugget leaves out. moran_z is a diagnostic of the cell means and not a count rule. It grows as the cells get finer than the range, because neighbouring cells then resemble each other, and it is near zero at the coarsest counts it is computed at whatever the data. It does not say how well the cells represent the response, so select_resolution() refuses it unless asked with diagnostic = TRUE, and summary() leaves it out unless it is named.

plot(prof)

Two behaviours are worth knowing before reading the numbers.

cp needs a nugget to have an interior optimum. On a smooth field the piecewise-constant approximation keeps improving as cells shrink, the penalty is too small to stop it, and the minimum lands wherever min_cell_n stops the ladder. The support ceiling is then doing the choosing, and select_resolution() flags it.

This fixture has a fitted nugget of 0.7 against a partial sill of 1.42, which is why cp turns around inside the ladder here.

reliability is highest at a coarse count, because bigger cells hold more points and average away more noise. Its maximum usually lies below the range floor, where cells are wider than the range. select_resolution() therefore reads it from the floor up, and what it returns is then the floor: a bound on the analysis, with the range choosing and not the curve. The next section is about spotting that.

Choosing, and the flat region

select_resolution() picks the level a criterion prefers and reports the band around it.

sel <- select_resolution(prof, criterion = "reliability")
sel
## Resolution by reliability: 17 cells
##   flat region : 17 to 18 (2 of 16 levels)
##   cells       : density-weighted k-means++ starts (power 1, 8 neighbours)
##   note        : the optimum is the range floor (area / range^2); the bound is
##                 choosing, not the criterion. Fewer cells would be wider than
##                 the range and average over more than one patch of the field.

sel$best is the optimum and sel$flat is every level within tol of it. Quote the band when you write the analysis up. tol is relative to the optimum’s value for cp and reliability, and relative to the criterion’s range for elbow and moran_z, whose optima can be zero.

Two flags say when a bound chose instead of the criterion:

c(at_floor = sel$at_floor, at_ceiling = sel$at_ceiling)
##   at_floor at_ceiling 
##       TRUE      FALSE

at_floor is TRUE here. Reliability wanted to keep going coarser and the correlation-range floor stopped it, so read the answer as at most this fine and take the number as a bound on the analysis, not as an optimum. The floor is a fact about the data, so the fix is a different question, not a different tol.

Criteria can prefer different levels while agreeing on a region. summary() on the profile reads the count criteria at once, and closes with the levels that every band contains:

summary(prof)
## Resolution picks: 3 criteria over 16 levels (2 to 55 cells)
## 
##   cells: density-weighted k-means++ starts (power 1, 8 neighbours)
## 
##    criterion best flat region levels in band
##           cp   44    35 to 55              3
##  reliability   17    17 to 18              2
##          loo   35    35 to 44              2
## 
##   reliability: the optimum is the range floor (area / range^2).
##   There the bound is choosing, not the criterion.
## 
##   picks span 17 to 44 cells (2.6x)
##   no level is in every flat region: the criteria disagree over the
##   whole ladder. plot() draws the curves they were read from.

A band is a set of levels, not an interval, because the criterion curves are not monotone: a band that skips a rung prints as a comma-separated list, while a solid run of 3 rungs prints as a range, as cp does with 35 to 55. Where the bands overlap you have a defensible set of levels, and the last line names it; attr(summary(prof), "common") returns the same levels for use in code, and attr(summary(prof), "bands") each criterion’s region in full. Where they do not overlap, the criteria are answering different questions and you have to say which one your analysis needs. An empty intersection is a result: it says this field has no single resolution that satisfies every way of asking.

The table is not a decision procedure, and nothing in the package picks among its criteria for you. Cross-validating a model at each suggested level is affordable, but it does not settle the question either: on a simulated field the level that won on cross-validated R2R^2 moved with the fold seed, and the coarsest grid won most often because its score had the widest spread, not because it was better.

What the ladder can support

The ladder runs from 2 cells to a ceiling the data impose. The profile records that ceiling and, beside it, a floor from the autocorrelation range.

str(attr(prof, "bounds"))
## List of 15
##  $ floor       : int 17
##  $ ceiling     : int 55
##  $ ceiling_from: chr "min_cell_n"
##  $ supported   : logi TRUE
##  $ area        : num 976371
##  $ range       : num 243
##  $ n           : int 500
##  $ n_sample    : int 500
##  $ n_distinct  : int 500
##  $ min_cell_n  : int 9
##  $ range_floor : logi FALSE
##  $ n_response  : int 500
##  $ n_scored    : int 500
##  $ levels_given: logi FALSE
##  $ predictors  : logi FALSE

The ceiling is floor(n / min_cell_n), with n the rows that carry a response when one is given, or the number of distinct locations when that is smaller (one short of it when no location repeats); ceiling_from says which. Past it the average cell holds too few points to estimate anything from, or k-means has more centres to place than distinct points. The floor is ceiling(area / range^2), from the fitted autocorrelation range: cells wider than the range average over more than one patch of the field, mixing values the field itself keeps apart. The range is an estimate, so by default the floor is reported and not applied: it is a level of the ladder, select_resolution(criterion = "reliability") reads from it up, and range_floor = TRUE starts the ladder there.

When the floor exceeds the ceiling, the data cannot support a tessellation that respects their own correlation structure. supported is FALSE, a warning says so, and the ladder still runs from 2 to the ceiling so the cost of each level stays visible. The usual causes are too few points for the extent, or a correlation range shorter than the spacing between observations.

Setting a size

Of the criteria above, all but loo score the plain mean of a cell. summarize_by_cell() reports beside it, by default, a pooled value: the cell’s mean pulled toward the mean of the 8 cells around it, by a weight that grows with the number of observations the cell holds (estimate = "pooled"; vignette("reporting") shows how to read and report one). For that value no criterion sets the count. A size does: the number of observations a cell is to hold on average, obs_per_cell. A size s on n observations is max(2, round(n / s)) cells.

The default profile is one size, 4.5, scored for the pooled value, and select_resolution() reads the count off it by that size. This is the call with nothing named but the response:

prof_default <- resolution_profile(pts, response_var = "z")
select_resolution(prof_default)
## Resolution by size: 111 cells
##   size        : 4.5 rows per cell asked (obs_per_cell); 500 rows / 111 cells = 4.50
##   cells       : density-weighted k-means++ starts (power 1, 8 neighbours)
##   estimate    : pooled toward the 8 nearest cells
##   at this size: 0.4% of the rows are alone in their cell; median own weight 0.54
##   loo         : 1.54 (one cell for the layer: 2.08)
##   note        : the count is set by obs_per_cell = 4.5, the caller's choice;
##                 no criterion chose it.

obs_per_cell puts the profile’s ladder in those terms, one level per size, with the centres fitted to every row. estimate names the cell value the profile scores, the pooled value unless it says otherwise:

prof_size <- resolution_profile(pts, response_var = "z",
                                obs_per_cell = c(12, 9, 6, 4.5, 3))
as.data.frame(prof_size)[, c("levels", "scored_per_cell", "loo",
                             "share_alone", "own_weight")]
##   levels scored_per_cell      loo share_alone own_weight
## 1     42       11.904762 1.566779       0.000  0.8143550
## 2     56        8.928571 1.525325       0.000  0.7413916
## 3     83        6.024096 1.461817       0.002  0.7197274
## 4    111        4.504505 1.423166       0.010  0.6473814
## 5    167        2.994012 1.429188       0.048  0.5621471

Three of the columns say what a size leaves a cell value to stand on.

  • loo is the leave-one-out error of the pooled value: each observation is predicted by the value of its cell computed without it, and the squared errors are averaged. It needs no variogram. sac = "auto", the default, fits none on a ladder of sizes, so cp and reliability are NA in this profile.
  • share_alone is the share of the observations that are the only one in their cell.
  • own_weight is the median weight a pooled value gives its cell’s own mean. At 1 the pooled values are the plain means; at 0 each is the mean of the cell’s neighbours.

At the size of the default profile this ladder has other centres, and so another loo, than that profile had: a profile draws the starts of its levels in turn from one random stream under seed, so a level’s centres depend on the other levels of the ladder.

select_resolution(criterion = "size") returns the level of a size. It searches for no optimum, so the result has no flat region and sits on no bound:

sel_size <- select_resolution(prof_size, criterion = "size",
                              obs_per_cell = 4.5)
sel_size
## Resolution by size: 111 cells
##   size        : 4.5 rows per cell asked (obs_per_cell); 500 rows / 111 cells = 4.50
##   cells       : density-weighted k-means++ starts (power 1, 8 neighbours)
##   estimate    : pooled toward the 8 nearest cells
##   at this size: 1.0% of the rows are alone in their cell; median own weight 0.65
##   loo         : 1.42 (one cell for the layer: 2.08)
##   note        : the count is set by obs_per_cell = 4.5, the caller's choice;
##                 no criterion chose it.

loo is in the table to compare sizes by, not to choose one. For pooled values it tends to keep falling as the cells shrink, so its minimum tends to be the finest size offered, and the end of the ladder would then be choosing. On 200 simulated layers of 1,500 clustered observations of a field plus noise, profiled at seven sizes from 18 to 2, the lowest loo of the pooled value was at the size 2 on 176 (dev/sim-pooled-values.R in the package’s repository; ?resolution_profile gives the settings).

In the table above the lowest loo is at 111 cells, which is not the finest size offered: a tendency, not a rule.

The size is therefore the caller’s choice, made on other grounds: how many observations a cell value should stand on, which share_alone and own_weight describe. Under a size neither the cells, which are fitted to the coordinates, nor their number, which is a count of rows, depend on the response, so the count is not fitted to the values it will summarise.

A size does not ask whether the response has spatial structure the cells can use, so the selection asks it separately. structured is FALSE when one mean for the whole layer predicts a left-out observation as well as the cells do. The count stands either way, since the caller set it, and the functions that take the selection as a count then warn (class spatialkit_no_structure) that the cell values will say little that one mean does not.

data.frame(structured = sel_size$structured, loo = sel_size$loo,
           one_mean = sel_size$loo_one_cell)
##   structured      loo one_mean
## 1       TRUE 1.423166 2.081281

The selection goes to get_voronoi_seeds(), as in “Next” below. It carries a record of how the count was set, sel_size$count_rule, which the seeds, the cells and the assigned layer hand on to summarize_by_cell(). The summary then checks that it reports the cell value the count was chosen for, on the cells and rows that were scored.

Leave-one-out for plain means

With plain means the leave-one-out error does choose a count. Each observation is predicted by the mean of the other observations of its cell, or, when it is alone in its cell, by the mean of the cell of its nearest other observation. estimate = "mean" scores that error in the profile, and the default obs_per_cell = "auto" then offers the seven sizes 18, 12, 9, 6, 4.5, 3 and 2:

prof_loo <- resolution_profile(pts, response_var = "z", estimate = "mean")
as.data.frame(prof_loo)[, c("levels", "scored_per_cell", "loo", "loo_se",
                            "share_alone")]
##   levels scored_per_cell      loo    loo_se share_alone
## 1     28       17.857143 1.640425 0.1004998       0.000
## 2     42       11.904762 1.601586 0.1024429       0.000
## 3     56        8.928571 1.632183 0.1013714       0.000
## 4     83        6.024096 1.645847 0.1004743       0.000
## 5    111        4.504505 1.664467 0.1014937       0.004
## 6    167        2.994012 1.600161 0.1032003       0.050
## 7    250        2.000000 2.008358 0.1222162       0.174
sel_loo <- select_resolution(prof_loo, criterion = "loo")
sel_loo
## Resolution by loo: 167 cells
##   flat region : 42, 167 (2 of 7 levels)
##   cells       : density-weighted k-means++ starts (power 1, 8 neighbours)
##   estimate    : plain means
##   at this size: 5.0% of the rows are alone in their cell
##   loo         : 1.6 (one cell for the layer: 2.08)

The lowest error is at 167 cells, inside the sizes offered, so the criterion chose it.

sel_loo$flat is every level whose error is within tol of the lowest, and it is the answer to quote, as for any criterion. loo_se is the standard error of one level’s mean squared error. It is not the standard error of the difference between two levels: their errors come from the same observations.

Three things to know before relying on this criterion. The count now depends on the values of the response, so the next section applies, and select_on = "split" reads loo on one half of the layer. The error describes locations among the observations: it compares counts where data are near, and says nothing about the error of a map away from them. And it sets the count of plain means only; for pooled values a size does, as above. In the simulation of that section the lowest loo of the plain mean was at the finest size on none of the 200 layers: it was at 6 observations per cell on 86 of them, at 4.5 on 51 and at 9 on 49.

criterion = "auto" is the rule that goes with the profile’s estimate: "size" for pooled values and "loo" for plain means. It is select_resolution()‘s default, and a profile built with estimate and passed straight to get_voronoi_seeds() as n is read the same way. criterion = "cp" reads Mallows’ Cp, which neither profile of these two sections has, since neither fitted a variogram.

Choosing on one half, estimating on the other

Picking the level from the same response you then aggregate is a form of double-dipping: the cell count was chosen to suit one realisation of the field. select_on = "split" profiles part of the layer and hands back the row positions of both parts.

prof_split <- resolution_profile(pts, response_var = "z", n_levels = 16,
                                 select_on = "split")
sp <- attr(prof_split, "split")
sp
## Spatial half-split (block_kfold, seed 123): 251 selection rows, 249 estimation rows
##   $selection and $estimation are row positions in the layer as passed.

The split is spatially blocked, not random, and records the method and seed that produced it. A random half would put neighbours of every selection point in the estimation set, and on an autocorrelated field that leaks the structure you are choosing against. Blocking reduces that leak without removing it: the two halves share a border, and points on either side of it within the correlation range are still correlated, so read the separation as a large improvement on a random half rather than as independence.

Choose from prof_split, then aggregate the rows in sp$estimation. The cells on the ladder are still drawn on every point, so the count it picks is a count for the whole layer, and the ladder is as long as the full profile’s. Only the steps that read the response (the variogram, cp, moran_z, loo) use the selection half. The cost is power: those criteria see half the data, so the profile is noisier and the band wider. The estimation rows also fill only their own half of the layer: a cell inside the selection half gets none of them, and a cell across the border between the halves is estimated from the part of it on the estimation side. Read standard errors only off cells whose points are all estimation rows.

unlist(attr(prof_split, "bounds")[c("floor", "ceiling", "n", "supported")])
##     floor   ceiling         n supported 
##        21        55       500         1

The floor can differ from the full profile’s, because it comes from the range estimated on the selection half.

Next

Hand the selection to whichever call decides the cell count. For a Voronoi tessellation that is get_voronoi_seeds(). Given the select_resolution() result itself, it returns the centres of the partition the profile scored, and a k-means partition, weighted or not, is the Voronoi partition of its centres, so the cells built on those seeds are the cells the criteria judged; the bare count sel$best would run a new k-means, whose cells are not. This selection sits on the range floor, so the call warns that a bound chose the count (class spatialkit_bound_chosen; warnings are not shown in this article). build_tessellation() then works on the seeds:

bnd   <- clip_target_for(pts, expand = 0.02, quiet = TRUE)
seeds <- get_voronoi_seeds(boundary = bnd, method = "kmeans", n = sel,
                           sample_points = pts)
cells <- build_tessellation(seeds, boundary = bnd, method = "voronoi",
                            quiet = TRUE)
nrow(cells$cells)
## [1] 17

For a lattice the count goes to build_tessellation() itself, and the points go in directly:

hex <- build_tessellation(pts, boundary = bnd, method = "hex",
                          approx_n_cells = sel$best, quiet = TRUE)
nrow(hex$cells)
## [1] 27

The hex count overshoots the request: the target is adjusted for packing density and then clipped to an irregular boundary, so approx_n_cells is approximate in both directions. The seeded Voronoi hits the number exactly, because the seeds are the cells.

Passing approx_n_cells with method = "voronoi" warns and is ignored. Without the seeding step you get one cell per observation, which is a nearest-neighbour interpolation rather than a resolution.

vignette("spatialkit_nc_demo") runs the whole pipeline on real boundaries. ?resolution_profile documents how each criterion behaved on simulated fields, with the references; ?determine_optimal_levels covers the k-means++ restart budget and the nine-cell floor below which the model-aware criteria carry no information.
